text:
In late August 1854, cholera struck the crowded Soho district of London with terrifying speed. Within three days, more than a hundred people living near Broad Street were dead. Within ten days, around 500 had died. Many residents fled. Shops and homes stood shuttered. Cholera is a disease that causes violent diarrhea and rapid dehydration, and in those days it could kill a healthy adult within a day.

Nobody knew what caused it. The dominant belief was the miasma theory: that disease spread through foul air rising from rotting matter, sewage and filth. London in the 1850s certainly smelled bad enough to make this seem plausible. Germs had not yet been shown to cause disease, and the word "bacteria" meant little to most doctors.

John Snow, a physician who lived and worked a short walk from Broad Street, doubted the miasma explanation. He was an unusual man for his profession: a teetotaller and vegetarian, known for pioneering the use of anaesthesia, and he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He had also been thinking about cholera for years. During an earlier epidemic in 1848-49, he had noticed that the disease first showed itself in the gut, not the lungs. If people were breathing in a poison, he reasoned, why would the illness begin in the stomach and bowels? It made more sense that people were swallowing something. He suspected contaminated water.

When the Broad Street outbreak began, Snow did what few of his contemporaries thought to do. He went door to door. He walked the streets, asked who had died, where they had lived, and what they had been drinking. The deaths, he found, clustered tightly around one spot: a public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew water for cooking and drinking.

Snow drew a map. On a street plan of Soho he marked each death with a small black bar stacked at the address where it happened. The bars piled up around the Broad Street pump like a gathering storm. Maps of disease were not new, but Snow used his to make an argument, and the pattern was hard to ignore.

He also looked for the exceptions, which proved more revealing than the rule. A workhouse nearby housed about 535 people, yet only five died. Snow learned that the workhouse had its own well and never used the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the street had almost no cases either. Its workers were given free beer, and they also had their own well. Meanwhile, a widow living far away in Hampstead died of cholera. Snow discovered that she had once lived in Soho and liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it delivered to her every day. A niece who drank from the same bottle died too.

On 7 September, Snow took his evidence to the local Board of Guardians. They were not convinced of his theory, but they were willing to act. The next day, the handle was removed from the Broad Street pump, so that no one could draw water from it.

The outbreak was already declining by then, as many residents had fled and many of the most vulnerable were already dead. Because of this, the removal of the handle has sometimes been credited with more than it did. But Snow's real achievement lay elsewhere.

Later, the Reverend Henry Whitehead, a local curate who had been skeptical of Snow's theory, joined the investigation. Whitehead knew the neighbourhood and its people far better than Snow did. His own inquiries turned up the likely start of the outbreak: a baby girl who lived at 40 Broad Street had fallen ill with diarrhea shortly before the epidemic began. Her family's cesspool, it turned out, lay very close to the pump well, and its brickwork was found to be leaking. The infant's waste had apparently seeped into the water that hundreds of neighbours drank. Whitehead became a convert to Snow's view.

Snow had also made a larger study of cholera deaths across south London, comparing households served by two water companies. One drew its water from a stretch of the Thames downstream of the city's sewage; the other had moved its intake upstream, to cleaner water. The households supplied by the first company suffered far more deaths. It was a natural experiment, and a powerful one.

Official bodies were slow to accept his conclusions. A committee investigating the outbreak rejected the idea that the pump was to blame. Snow died in 1858, at only 45, still without wide acceptance of his theory. Yet over the following years, as microscopes improved and the germ theory of disease took hold, his work was vindicated. Cholera is indeed carried by a bacterium, spread through contaminated water.

Snow's legacy reaches well beyond cholera. By gathering data, mapping it and comparing groups, he showed how to find the cause of a disease without yet understanding it fully. Many consider him a founder of modern epidemiology, the science of how diseases spread through populations. The principles he used, careful counting, looking for patterns, and testing explanations against the exceptions, are still how public health detectives work today.
